title: Bees in the City
intro: You should spend about 20 minutes on this passage.

paras.t: In the early 2000s, a beekeeper in a large northern city placed two hives on the roof of an office block and waited to see what would happen. By the end of the summer, each hive had produced more honey than the average hive on a farm thirty kilometres away. The result surprised him, and it was soon repeated by others. Today hives can be found on the roofs of hotels, hospitals and department stores, and in some countries the number of urban beekeepers has doubled in a decade.

The explanation lies in what a city offers a bee. Modern farmland is often a desert for pollinators: huge fields of a single crop flower for only a few weeks, and the margins between fields have been cleared to make room for machinery. A city, by contrast, is a patchwork of parks, gardens, window boxes, cemeteries and railway embankments, and something is in flower for most of the year. Lime trees, which line many European streets, are especially valuable, since a single tree can supply nectar for several hives during its short flowering season.

Pesticides are the second advantage. Farmers who spray their crops may unintentionally poison the bees that feed on them, whereas most city authorities have restricted or banned the use of the strongest chemicals in public parks. Warmth also helps. Because buildings and roads store heat, a city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside, which allows colonies to begin foraging earlier in spring and to continue later into autumn.

The honey itself has attracted attention. Because bees from a single hive visit many different plants, urban honey tends to have a complex flavour that changes from street to street and from month to month. In one project, a group of chefs and a university laboratory compared samples from fourteen districts of a single city and found that no two jars tasted the same. Some producers now label their honey with the name of the neighbourhood, in the same way that winemakers label bottles with the name of a vineyard. Researchers have also tested city honey for heavy metals such as lead; the levels were generally lower than the limits set for food safety, because bees filter much of what they carry and because leaded petrol has long been banned.

Not everyone is persuaded that the boom is good news. Dr Imogen Hale, an ecologist, argues that honeybees are only one of more than two hundred bee species found in a typical European country, and that most of the others are wild, solitary insects that nest in the ground or in dead wood. Her team counted wild bees on flowering plants in thirty city parks and discovered that, in parks containing several hives, the wild bees were fewer and visited the flowers less often. "A city can only produce so much nectar," she says. "If we keep adding hives, the honeybees take a growing share and the wild species go hungry."

Beekeepers accept that hive numbers need limits, but they question how far her findings can be generalised. The parks in the study were small, they point out, and the survey lasted a single summer. Some of them also argue that the bigger threat to wild bees is the loss of nesting sites, not competition for food. A few councils have started to respond by encouraging the planting of flowers that produce nectar over a long season, and by leaving small areas of grass uncut so that wild bees can nest there.

A sensible middle path is beginning to emerge. Guidelines drawn up by one city council suggest that only a fixed number of hives should be kept within a given distance of each other, and that anyone wanting to keep bees must complete a short training course first. Educators have taken up the cause too: several schools now run hives as part of their science lessons, and children who have watched a colony at work often become the most enthusiastic defenders of all insects, not only the honeybee. If that attitude spreads, the city may prove to be a refuge for far more than the honeybee alone.

items.s: The first rooftop hives described in the passage gave more honey than a typical hive on a nearby farm.
e: each hive had produced more honey than the average hive on a farm thirty kilometres away

items.s: Most farmland gives bees flowers to feed on all year round.
e: huge fields of a single crop flower for only a few weeks

items.s: Lime trees flower for a long period each year.
City authorities have banned every pesticide in public parks.
e: restricted or banned the use of the strongest chemicals in public parks

items.s: Tests found dangerous levels of lead in city honey.
e: the levels were generally lower than the limits set for food safety

items.s: The honey comparison project was paid for by a food company.
e: a group of chefs and a university laboratory compared samples from fourteen districts
items.w: The passage names the people who ran the project but never says who paid for it.

items.s: Dr Hale's team studied wild bees in thirty city parks.
e: counted wild bees on flowering plants in thirty city parks

items.s: Dr Hale thinks beekeepers should need a licence.
e: If we keep adding hives, the honeybees take a growing share
items.w: She warns about too many hives but never mentions licences.

items.s: The park survey continued for more than one summer.
e: the survey lasted a single summer

items.s: Some beekeepers consider a shortage of nesting sites a greater danger to wild bees than competition for food.
e: the bigger threat to wild bees is the loss of nesting sites, not competition for food

items.q: According to paragraph B, farmland is a poor habitat for bees because
o: flowers there bloom briefly and the edges of fields have been removed
farm machinery frightens bees away from the crops
most crops are grown without any flowers
fields are too large for bees to cross
e: flower for only a few weeks, and the margins between fields have been cleared

items.q: City colonies can start foraging earlier in spring because
o: plants in cities are watered more often
buildings and roads keep the city warmer
there are fewer birds that eat bees
hives on roofs receive more sunlight
e: Because buildings and roads store heat, a city can be several degrees warmer

items.q: What do some beekeepers say about Dr Hale's research?
o: It was paid for by farmers.
It ignored the wild bees in small parks.
It may not apply to every situation.
It proved that hives should be banned.
e: The parks in the study were small, they point out, and the survey lasted a single summer
